item.title: Yes, I'm still alive.
item.content:encoded:
While I did find this incredibly intriguing/engaging/mysterious, I'm still curious about the two entries in the second disk: The Camel and the Gecko. If you were missing large portions of your body and bleeding profusely, I'm pretty sure thirty seconds would be a stretch of a lifespan for something that small, however the gecko survives for a minute afterwards and only perishes once its jugular had been severed. Secondly, How does a camel not notice its innards being devoured? Surely it would have stood up long before it actually did or died before it could notice.

I'm not saying that those entries don't belong in the tale, (I think they help accentuate the overall creepy factor.) just that they aren't explained very well and no similar events occur later on. In both cases the (fictional representations of real animals) live for far longer than they should have. (that camel could still be alive and well as a matter of fact.)

This also kind of works. Taking the whole nature reserve theory into account, it could be that the curators don't want to lose the rare and endangered species within.

item.content:encoded: Actually that's a bad example of a jump cut. The camera's position has to vary slightly, so a better example would be a shot of a guy in a chair that cuts to a shot of the same guy in the same chair but the camera has moved 6 feet to the left or has zoomed in.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: I'm not sure you are using the term "jump cut" correctly. Video transitions can fade, dissolve, wipe, and cut. A cut is simply when one shot ends and another begins on the next frame. A jump cut is when the next shot is very similar to the previous one, such as when you leave the camera in a fixed location but cut to a later time, resulting in a very similar shot but maybe the shadows are longer and there's suddenly someone sitting in a previously empty chair. When the first shot cuts to a second shot that is completely different, like from a guy handling a snake to an anthill, it's called a simple cut (or just a cut)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I know this tale is all about biology gone wrong, but there are quite a few places where small clarifications would make this stronger, especially considering that the Foundation personnel involved in writing this were biologists (as well as A/V guys).

For example:
- Trilobites are not insects.
- There is more than one species of diamondback rattlesnake.
- Redwood trees aren't found in the American southwest, which of course could be the point. However, the way the sentence is written makes me think the presence of the redwoods is taken as evidence for determining the SW as the locale.
- Utahraptor is the name of genus and thus should be italicized, but since it's written in an italicized note, I believe the convention would be to unitalicize it. Or maybe underline, I'm not sure.
- Megatherium is a genus of giant ground sloth. A "Megalotherium" … isn't anything at all any more, actually: it was a term was coined in 1889 by Lydekker. Lydekker shortly thereafter realized that Cuvier had already described the sloths back in 1796. Thus, Cuiver's name, Megatherium, has precedence. Lydekker corrected his mistake, making Megalotherium a junior synonym of Megatherium.
- They could ID the snake but not the lizard? Not even to family?
